w: Every periodontal surgery sits somewhere on one spectrum: a simple extraction might need no incision and no flap at all; a soft-tissue graft over a recession needs a small flap with limited reflection; a sinus or ridge augmentation needs a large flap opened by multiple incisions. The choice of incision and flap design is genuinely clinician-dependent — Dr. Basma was upfront that two surgeons can disagree on the best approach to the same case — but a small, fixed set of designs covers nearly everything. Naming an incision: it's about the tooth, not the technique The most-missed distinction in this session is that intrasulcular and crestal describe the same physical incision, named differently only by whether a tooth is present. If a tooth is there, the blade is inserted in the sulcus to separate the gingival fibers from the tooth — all the way around, buccal, lingual, and through the papillae — and that's called intrasulcular. If the site is edentulous, there's no sulcus, so the identical straight incision along the crest of the ridge is instead called a crestal incision. More teeth included in the intrasulcular/crestal incision means more flap and better access, but including teeth you don't need to compromises esthetics for no benefit. When intrasulcular or crestal alone doesn't give enough exposure — most major augmentations — a vertical (releasing) incision is dropped at the line angle of a tooth to open a bigger flap without having to include more teeth in the horizontal incision. One vertical incision plus intrasulcular across three teeth (say, distal of #7 with intrasulcular on 7-8-9) makes a triangular pyramidal flap — enough exposure for implant placement with an onlay graft. Two verticals, one on each side of the defect, make a trapezoidal flap, needed for major vertical augmentation because two releases let the flap coronally advance with passive, tension-free closure over a graft — something a single vertical often can't stretch to do without tearing. There's one more incision family that skips reflection almost entirely: the envelope (pouch) flap. The papillae are never touched — only the buccal tissue is elevated, giving just enough release to coronally advance the flap over a soft-tissue graft (autogenous or allograft) while leaving the interdental architecture completely intact. This is the design of choice for pure root-coverage cases, where disturbing the papilla would work against the esthetic goal. Reading a flap design Beyond how it's opened, a flap is classified along three more axes: how much bone is exposed on reflection (full-thickness, taking the periosteum with it, versus split-thickness, leaving periosteum on the bone), where it's repositioned after surgery (coronal to the CEJ for soft-tissue augmentation, or apical for crown lengthening and osseous surgery), and whether the papilla is preserved intact or not. A sulcular flap — intrasulcular incision only, no vertical release — gives the most limited access of the group and is hard to advance because the tissue stays attached laterally; it's the first, smallest option, reached for on minor augmentation or a single implant. Extending it to include one more tooth on each side (still no vertical) buys moderate additional access without escalating to a releasing incision at all. The full-vs-split decision has a simple test behind it: if the surgical goal involves bone in any way, reflect full thickness and expose it; if the goal is purely soft tissue, go split thickness and leave the periosteum behind as a vascularized bed. That single rule covers every case the course walks through — implant placement, bone/ridge/sinus augmentation, and crown lengthening or osseous surgery (all bone-related) are full-thickness; soft-tissue grafting is the one split-thickness exception, precisely because a split-thickness bed is what lets the graft's blood vessels anastomose with the recipient site's own vessels during healing. A fourth incision: sub-marginal, for eliminating a pocket The in-class review added a fourth named incision that doesn't fit the reflect-and-close pattern of the other three: the sub-marginal incision, placed below the free gingival margin (the "sub" is literal — below the margin) rather than in the sulcus or on the crest. Where intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions are about gaining access and are designed to be closed back to their original position, a sub-marginal incision is deliberately excisional: it's scalloped through the pocket wall itself and the tissue coronal to it is removed outright, not reflected and repositioned. The point is pocket elimination in resective/osseous surgery — if a site probes 6 mm against a 3 mm normal, cutting roughly 3 mm of pocket wall away leaves the patient with a shallower, cleansable sulcus instead of a deep one that will keep repopulating with pathogens between maintenance visits. The tradeoff is intentional: this incision creates recession by design (the gingival margin ends up higher after healing), which is the right call when the alternative is an unmaintainable periodontal pocket, but the wrong call — and never attempted — on a site being treated for recession instead of pocket depth. Whether recession should be created or corrected at a given site always comes back to what the actual problem is: a deep pocket calls for a sub-marginal incision, thin/receded tissue calls for grafting, and the two aren't contradictory approaches, just answers to different problems. Choosing a suture material At the broadest level, sutures split into absorbable (degrade in the body via hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage — gut, chromic gut, and the synthetic Vicryl/Monocryl family) and non-absorbable (must be physically removed by the clinician, typically 10–14 days out, or left long-term — silk, ePTFE, polypropylene/Prolene, nylon). Plain gut resorbs fastest (7–10 days); chromic gut, treated with chromium salts, lasts a bit longer (10–14 days); synthetic absorbables like Vicryl hold tensile strength for 2–3 weeks and fully resorb over a longer stretch. Absorbables are the natural choice for quick pediatric cases or simple extractions where a suture-removal visit is a burden; non-absorbables like ePTFE are favored over major bone grafts specifically because they resist plaque attraction, hold high tensile strength, and won't break down prematurely on you. The course's own material comparison chart sorts six specific materials along the same two axes — natural vs. synthetic, monofilament vs. braided — plus resorption time, strength, tissue reaction, and handling (full chart in Reference Tables). Chromic gut is natural, monofilament, and resorbs fastest (7–10 days) but handles very poorly; it's reached for at extraction sites, implants without additional grafting, or to stabilize a collagen membrane. The two synthetic resorbables split by construction: PGA is braided, resorbs slowest of the resorbables (55–70 days), handles beautifully, but irritates tissue — a fit for ridge and sinus augmentation where healing takes a while. PGCL is monofilament, resorbs faster (22–55 days), and is gentler on tissue, making it the choice for soft-tissue grafting and esthetic crown lengthening. Among the non-resorbables, poly-propylene behaves like nylon with no tissue adherence; silk handles beautifully but causes the worst tissue reaction of any material on the list and must be physically removed at 7 days; PTFE is the highest-cost option and is used across nearly every surgery type except pure soft-tissue grafts. The monofilament-vs-braided split isn't just a handling preference — it's an infection-control decision. A braided suture's woven strands wick and trap bacteria the way a monofilament's smooth single strand doesn't, which is exactly the mechanism behind silk's poor tissue-reaction score. Whenever a braided suture is used and has to come out, wipe it down with chlorhexidine-soaked gauze before removing it: pulling a plaque-coated braided suture back out through the flap can drag that plaque into the wound on the way out. Grafting from the palate: donor-site selection and protection Keratinized tissue (pale pink, firm, immobile) is what protects the periodontium against the mechanical trauma of chewing, the way keratinized skin protects a fall better than thin mucosa does; non-keratinized tissue (red, thin, mobile, heavily vascular) can't take that load. When a site lacks adequate keratinized tissue around a tooth or implant, the fix is a graft, and the palate is the best universal donor source because it's uniformly firm, keratinized, immobile tissue. Donor-site selection within the palate still matters: harvest from the molar area rather than the premolar area, because the premolar region carries proportionally more fatty adipose tissue beneath the epithelium, and adipose tissue resorbs quickly once transplanted — a graft that includes too much of it will visibly shrink. The palate's tissue layers, from the surface down, are epithelium, then connective tissue (lamina propria), then adipose tissue over bone; a connective tissue graft keeps only the middle layer; the epithelium is trimmed away and the fatty layer is avoided by design, not just as an unavoidable leftover. Grafting works because two cut, epithelium-free surfaces held in contact will anastomose their blood vessels and heal together — the same reason two cut fingers held together will reattach, but two fingers merely pressed together (epithelium intact) never will. That's also why the recipient site is prepared as a split-thickness bed: the periosteum left behind gives the graft a vascularized surface to fuse to. The donor site itself is left as an open wound on the roof of the mouth, which is genuinely painful (described in class as comparable to a bad pizza burn, since every swallow and sip exposes raw nerve endings) — management options are a composite-resin stent placed before harvest to preserve the palatal contour of the defect, PRF placed over the wound, or a custom palatal stent/night guard the patient wears for a minimum of three days while the site re-epithelializes, removed only to clean and then replaced. Watch for the greater palatine artery in this area — hitting it is the most common source of problematic bleeding during palatal harvest. Needle geometry matters as much as the thread. A reverse cutting needle keeps its flat side toward the tissue on the upward pass, reducing tear-through compared to a standard cutting needle. Larger curvature (a bigger arc of the circle) takes a deeper bite; a larger needle diameter passes through more tissue but demands more hand rotation. In suture sizing, a larger number means a smaller diameter — and a smaller-diameter thread needs more knots to hold securely. Choosing a technique Single interrupted sutures (with the figure-8 variant) are the general-purpose default, each throw tied independently. Horizontal mattress sutures are essential for larger bone-augmentation procedures and prevent flap-margin inversion, but overtightening constricts blood supply to the incision edge and risks bone necrosis and dehiscence. Vertical mattress sutures maximize tissue approximation and eversion, and are the go-to for approximating papillae in the esthetic zone or closing an oro-antral communication. Continuous and continuous-locking sutures place bites close together for a strong seal, but the entire line can come undone if a single throw fails — a real risk with monofilament or other high-glide materials — and are typically reserved for edentulous long-span areas, alveoloplasties, and apicoectomies. Sling and periosteal-anchorage sutures round out the technique list for repositioning a flap around a single tooth or anchoring it apically or laterally. Five surgical principles Every incision and flap in this course answers to the same five rules: a firm, continuous stroke rather than several tentative passes; keeping the incision at a distance from the actual lesion or bony defect rather than cutting directly over it; placing vertical incisions at the line angle of the tooth; reflecting the periosteum as an integral part of the flap; and keeping the base of the flap at least as wide as its free edge, since a narrow base starves the flap of the only blood supply it has left once it's reflected. Periodontal-orthodontic clearance: when a referring orthodontist plans to move already-thin-tissue incisors further buccally, get ahead of it — a prophylactic soft-tissue graft to thicken the tissue first prevents the recession that pushing a tooth through thin buccal bone/tissue tends to cause, rather than waiting to treat the recession afterward. The best time to treat recession is always the earliest one.
